title: Tesla remote operators keep crashing its ‘Robotaxis,’ data shows
key_facts: Tesla's latest crash reports to the US safety regulator NHTSA add two more Robotaxi crashes in which a remote operator, not the car's software, was driving.
That makes five such crashes in the data; each ended in a collision. Tesla now has 36 unique Robotaxi incident reports, up from 22 in July.
The two new crashes were in August: Dallas (about 0.40 mph, hit a parked SUV) and Austin (about 1 mph, hit a dumpster); no passengers aboard, property damage only.
Two earlier ones, in July 2025 and January 2026 in Austin, were at 8 and 9 mph.
Tesla does not disclose how often remote operators intervene, so no rate can be calculated.
Waymo wrote in a February 2026 letter to Senator Ed Markey that it has not used remote driving where a human performs the driving task.
quote_evidence: Tesla now has 36 unique “Robotaxi” incident reports on file, up from 22 when we last looked at this in July.
Tesla doesn’t disclose how often remote operators intervene, so there’s no way to calculate a rate.
Nobody’s been hurt, and we’re talking about bumpers, a dumpster, and a tree stump at walking speed.
why_it_matters_hint: Shows how often robotaxis still need a human to rescue them, and how that rescue has gone.
event_date: Crashes in August 2026 (also Jul 2025, Jan 2026); in NHTSA September data release
notes: Electrek's own analysis of NHTSA data; the article mixes reporting with opinion, only the data-based facts used. Crash events are older than 15 Oct, so score lowered by 1.
